Introduction

Business Process Management (BPM) engines are a critical backbone for modern automation platforms, but they are often constrained by performance, scalability, and infrastructure cost. TaktX was built to address these challenges directly: a lean, horizontally scalable and fault tolerant BPMN engine designed from the ground up for high throughput and low latency.

This benchmark report presents the first systematic performance results of TaktX under twoscenarios:

  • Raw throughput — a trivial “no wait state” process definition, designed to test the maximumexecution speed of the engine.
  • Sustained throughput — a “typical” business process containing service tasks, timers, and a gateway, designed to represent real-world workloads.

The goal of these benchmarks is to demonstrate not only the raw processing ceiling of TaktX, but also its ability to sustain many concurrent process instances with predictable near-real-time latency and near-linear scalability — even on modest cloud infrastructure. It also shows eﬃcient storage; thanks to a compact binary message format and lean persistence, TaktX stores far more instance state per GB than other engines

Global architecture of this test

Design goal.

TaktX is a Kafka-native BPMN engine optimized for high throughput on modest hardware. Execution is fully event-driven; state transitions are written to a durable log and processed in parallel across partitions. By using Kafka we gain the capabilities of a fully horizontally scalable and fault tolerant engine.

Core components

  • Engine nodes (stateless compute): Execute BPMN semantics, advance tokens, and emit commands/events. Kafka Streams–based runtime with N threads per node. For this test all local state was stored in memory with the Kafka change-logs as backup.
  • Broker cluster: Kafka cluster with topics for process definition-commands, process instance-commands, timer-schedules, update-stream (broadcast/exports) and change-logs for persistence of state. Note: no other databases are used for processing. Kafka is the only “source of truth” for all engine, worker and other client nodes.
  • Workers: External task executors (for service tasks). In the “typical” benchmark they simulate 200ms work per task.
  • Starter / Load generator: Produces start commands according to a target rate.
  • Observability: Metrics and latency percentiles from engine and workers; optional broadcaststream for UI/analytics.

Execution & data flow (simplified)

  1. Start. Starter writes StartProcess commands → consumed by an engine node assigned to that partition.
  2. Engine step: Engine validates & advances tokens, emits instance update events.
  3. Service tasks: Workers consume service task commands, perform work, then emit completed events → engine consumes and advances the token.
  4. Timers: Engine writes timer due-dates into timer-schedule (time-bucketed). When buckets elapse, due timers are emitted and processed to resume execution.
  5. Completion: Engine writes final state and (optionally) an update on the instance-updates stream.

Durability & delivery

  • Writes use acks=all + idempotent producers; engine processing is at-least-once with idempotent state transitions
  • Fault tolerance: If an engine node fails, Kafka partition leadership reassignment + consumer rebalancing moves processing; state is reconstructed from the log and local caches warm quickly.

Scalability model

  • Horizontal scale: by increasing partitions and engine nodes. Throughput tracks partition parallelism; adding threads beyond partition count provides no gain.
  • Work isolation: Activities remain bound to the partition that owns their process instance, minimizing cross-partition chatter.
  • Partition per job-worker: Having a separate topic for each job-worker type allows for fine-grained control of scaling partitions. Heavily used job-workers can communicate over topics with more partitions than other less used workers.

Security

  • Transport encryption via TLS; credentials via SASL.
  • By fully using Kafka to persist state it becomes very easy to implement end-to-end security for data at rest (planned premium feature).

Observability & export cost

An optional instance-update broadcast feeds UI/analytics. Disabling it (“running headless”) reduced overhead ~20–30% in the raw tests; sustained tests ran with broadcast on.

Why this matters for benchmarks

The architecture explains the near-linear scaling with partitions and why latency remains sub-second until saturation. It also clarifies that results were achieved with durability on, and why broadcast slightly lowers the raw ceiling.
